title: One $20 AI subscription for my Unity ARPG: coding or 3D assets?
author: UsefulGuest266
selftext:
For my solo Unity ARPG, Codex makes more sense when I’m dealing with C# scripts, enemy AI, or getting combat mechanics to work properly. But once I get to building out levels, the bottleneck changes. Say I’m making a ruined village that’s been swallowed by giant tree roots. There’s a shrine built into one of them, a watchtower twisted around another, and a bunch of smaller objects that need to follow the same visual style. That’s where Meshy Pro starts looking more useful. I could generate base models from my concept images, then adjust and combine them in Blender instead of building every custom shape from scratch.

The part I’m less sure about is characters. A generated enemy might look great in a preview, but then you give it a weapon, play an attack animation, and suddenly the shoulder bends strangely or the armor clips through the body. Now you’re back in Blender fixing things.

Maybe the sensible move is to pay for coding help while the systems are unfinished, then switch to 3D generation when there’s an actual world to populate.

Do other solo devs rotate subscriptions like this, or just keep everything active?

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I'm only paying for Claude. It and others like it can use Blender MCP to do some modelling. Combined with a Trellis2 workflow for mesh generation, and the NanoBanana 2 api from Google, I can give a concept image to Claude and it will break it up into pieces and model those, then try to put all the pieces back together. 

I wish these companies had a mid range tier. The low tiers of Claude and Tripo run out too quickly, and the high tiers are 5 times the price. Everyone seems to be doing it that way. So I chose Claude, but it can do a not so great imitation of what those modelling services do. I'm hoping I can keep refining it and making it better, but it's not as good as their low poly meshes. But I'd rather try to figure it out myself anyway, with this rather expensive Claude Max subscription that is making the others unaffordable.

comments.author: Chengzhong_PR
comments.body: For me any visual work (2d/3d model, arts, UI) by AI, I find Codex does a better job, but other things especially coding I leave to Claude Opus 5.5.

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
Rotating makes sense to me, and I'd lean into it by batching. While the systems are unfinished, block the village out with gray boxes and keep a running list of every prop and building you end up wanting, then pay for the 3D tool for one month and work through the whole list at once. You get more out of a month that way than from generating a shrine here and there between coding sessions, and the style stays more consistent when everything comes out of the same stretch of work.



For characters I'd split it differently. Static props forgive messy topology because nothing bends, but anything that deforms needs clean loops around the shoulders and hips, which is where generated meshes tend to fall apart. I'd keep enemies on a small number of properly rigged base bodies and use generation for the armor pieces and weapons that attach to them.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Coding. There are a million ways to get high quality free assets (or make them yourself). There are not a million ways to have AI help code your systems.

comments.author: daddy_reloaded
comments.body:
If you can only spend 20$ a month, then use it for coding only. 3d modeling with llm require a lot of usage, and it is clearly less efficient compare to coding. 

For the tripo/meshy part, I found it very efficient.  
When I use tripo, in general I build some parts independently (for tris control) and assemble them in blender (manually). I also rework the articulation vertices so it's better when animated. This part starts to be efficient with llm too, but honestly it takes few minutes manually. Rigging can be done with accuring for free, and it does a great job for a starting point.
Then the animations. If your mesh is well prepared, applying a mixamo animation is generally easy (of your character has also normal proportions).

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
Well, a game without 3D assets is still a game. Can be a 2D game.

3D assets and no code is not a game.

So definitely code first. I tried codex and Claude, but I'm getting by far the best results from the $20 plan from both. Claude does all the coding and Codex does all the asset generation. They work really well together. And when one runs out of energy I use the other one mainly. 

Codex does one other thing well, and that's project talking to eachother. So my games are talking to my tools, to improve the tools where needed.
